However,\ngenerations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the\ntextbook of \\ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of\nthe theorem,\nno proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.\nThat changed with the publication of\n\\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used\nGaussians.\nWalther's proof depends on\na nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \\over 2}$ pages of\ncalculations. See Section 8.7 of \\ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation\nof Walther's proof.\nBy contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids\ncalculations.\n\nA brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.\nUsing Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\\mu(S)$\nfor all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\\mu$-average distance $f_\\mu(x)$\nto every point, $x$.\nWe then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\\mu$\nyields a constant times $\\mu$.\nThus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\\mu$.\n\n\\bsection{Proof}{s.proof}\n\n\nLet $\\hfsp$ be the set of closed half-spaces $S \\subset\\R^n$.\n\n\\proclaim The Cram\\'er--Wold Theorem. Let $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ be Borel\nprobability measures on $\\R^n$ such that $\\mu(S) = \\nu(S)$ for all $S \\in\n\\hfsp$. Then $\\mu = \\nu$.\n\n\\proof\nLet\n$\\sigma$ be the (infinite) Borel measure on $\\hfsp$ \nthat is invariant under isometries, normalized so that\n$$\n\\sigma\\big(\\{0 \\in S, x \\notin S\\}\\big) = \\|x\\|/2\n\\label e.distance\n$$\nfor $\\|x\\|= 1$.\nThe measure $\\sigma$ goes back to \\ref b.Crofton/ (in two dimensions); it\ncan be constructed as follows. (See Theorem 5.1.1 of \\ref b.SW:book/ for\na generalization.)\nLet $\\sfc_{n-1}$ denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere\n$\\sphere^{n-1} \\subset \\R^n$, and let\n$\\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\\R$.\nWrite $\\varphi \\colon \\sphere^{n-1} \\times \\R \\to \\hfsp$ for the map\n$$\n\\varphi(\\omega, p)\n:=\n\\bigl\\{ x \\in \\R^n \\st \\ip \\omega, x \\ge p \\bigr\\}\n\\,.\n$$\nThen $\\sigma := \\alpha_n \\cdot \\varphi_*(\\sfc_{n-1} \\times \\lambda)$ for some\nconstant $\\alpha_n$ whose value does not concern us.\nIt is clear that $\\sigma$ is invariant under rotations about the origin\nand under reflections in hyperplanes that pass through the origin.\nTranslation invariance\namounts to the property that for $y \\in \\R^n$, the pushforward by\n$\\varphi_y(\\omega, p) := \\varphi(\\omega, p) - y$ is the same measure. But\nsince \n$$\\eqaln{\n\\varphi(\\omega, p) - y \n&= \n\\bigl\\{ x - y \\in \\R^n \\st \\ip \\omega, x \\ge p \\bigr\\}\n=\n\\bigl\\{ x \\in \\R^n \\st \\ip \\omega, {x + y} \\ge p \\bigr\\}\n\\cr&=\n\\bigl\\{ x \\in \\R^n \\st \\ip \\omega, x \\ge p - \\ip \\omega, y \\bigr\\}\n=\n\\varphi\\bigl(\\omega, p - \\ip \\omega, y\\bigr)\n\\,,\n}$$\nisometry invariance of $\\lambda$ gives this property.\nThe isometry invariance of $\\sigma$ implies that $\\sigma\\big(\\{0 \\in S,\\, x\n\\notin S\\}\\big)$ is a function of $\\|x\\|$ alone; additivity for collinear\nsegments shows that it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose $\\alpha_n$\nso that \\ref e.distance/ holds.\n\nFrom \\ref e.distance/ and isometry invariance, we have\n$$\n\\|x\\| =\n\\int_\\hfsp |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \\,d\\sigma(S)\n\\,.\n$$\nIntegrating with respect to a\nsigned measure $\\mu$ on $\\R^n$ with compact support, we obtain\n$$\n\\int_{\\R^n} \\|x\\| \\,d\\mu(x)\n=\n\\int_\\hfsp \\int_{\\R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \\,d\\mu(x) \\,d\\sigma(S)\n=\n\\int_\\hfsp \\Bigl[1_S(0)\\big(1 - 2\\mu(S)\\big) + \\mu(S)\\Bigr] \\,d\\sigma(S)\n\\,.\n$$\nThe choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another\nchoice and subtracting, we get\n$$\n\\int_{\\R^n} \\big(\\|y - x\\| - \\|x\\|\\big) \\,d\\mu(x)\n=\n\\int_\\hfsp \\Bigl[\\bigl(1_S(y) - 1_S(0)\\bigr)\\bigl(1 - 2\\mu(S)\\bigr)\\Bigr]\n\\,d\\sigma(S)\n\\,.\n$$\nBy taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed\nmeasure, $\\mu$.\n\nDefine\n$$\nf_\\mu(y)\n:=\n\\int_{\\R^n} \\big(\\|y - x\\| - \\|x\\|\\big) \\,d\\mu(x)\n\\,.\n$$\nWe have shown that the function $S \\mapsto \\mu(S)$ determines $f_\\mu$. It\nremains to show that $f_\\mu$ determines $\\mu$.\n\nThe idea is that if $n = 2m-1$ is odd, then $\\Delta^m f_\\mu = c_m\n\\mu$ for some constant $c_m$, using the fundamental solution of the\nLaplacian, $\\Delta$.    196	\int_\hfsp \Bigl[\bigl(1_S(y) - 1_S(0)\bigr)\bigl(1 - 2\mu(S)\bigr)\Bigr]
   197	\,d\sigma(S)
   198	\,.
   199	$$
   200	By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed
   201	measure, $\mu$.
   202	
   203	Define
   204	$$
   205	f_\mu(y)
   206	:=
   207	\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
   208	\,.
   209	$$
   210	We have shown that the function $S \mapsto \mu(S)$ determines $f_\mu$. It
   211	remains to show that $f_\mu$ determines $\mu$.
   212	
   213	The idea is that if $n = 2m-1$ is odd, then $\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m
   214	\mu$ for some constant $c_m$, using the fundamental solution of the
   215	Laplacian, $\Delta$. This then establishes the Cram\'er--Wold theorem
   216	in odd dimensions.
   217	But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension, 
   218	the Cram\'er--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well.
   219	That is, we may identify a measure $\mu$ on $\R^{2m}$ with a measure $\mu'$
   220	on $\R^{2m} \times \{0\} \subset \R^{2m+1}$. 
   221	%Note that values on closed
   222	%half-spaces determine values on open half-spaces by continuity.
   223	%Thus, 
   224	The function $S \mapsto
   225	\mu(S)$ on half-spaces $S \subset \R^{2m}$ determines the values
   226	$\mu'(S')$ for half-spaces $S' \subset \R^{2m+1}$. Since this determines
   227	$\mu'$, the theorem follows for $\mu$.
   228	
   229	\iffalse
   230	To prove this, it suffices to show that $f_\mu$
   231	determines $\int g \,d\mu$ for all $g \in C^\infty_{\csp}(\R^{2m-1})$. I claim
   232	that if $\Delta^m r = c_m \delta_0$, then $\int g \,d\mu = c_m^{-1}
   233	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y)$. Indeed,
   234	$$\eqaln{
   235	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y) 
   236	&=
   237	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} (\Delta^m g)(y) \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,
   238	d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
   239	\cr&=
   240	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} g(y) \Delta_y^m \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,
   241	d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
   242	\cr&=
   243	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} c_m g(x) \,d\mu(x)
   244	\,.
   245	}$$
   246	\fi
   247	
   248	We now show that
   249	$\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m \mu$ in an appropriate sense for $\mu$ on $\R^{2m-1}$.
   250	Recall Green's second identity, which says that for a
   251	bounded domain $D \subset \R^n$ with $C^1$ boundary $\partial D$ having
   252	outward unit normal $\n$ and two functions $\phi, \psi \in C^2(\overlinesl
   253	D\,)$, we
   254	have
   255	$$
   256	\int_D (\phi \Delta \psi - \psi \Delta \phi) 
   257	=
   258	\int_{\partial D} (\phi \nabla_\n \psi - \psi \nabla_\n \phi)
   259	\,.
   260	$$
   261	Recall also that if $F \colon \R^n \to \R$ is such that $F(x) =
   262	G\bigl(\|x\|\bigr)$ depends only on $r := \|x\|$, then 
   263	$$
   264	(\Delta F)(x)
   265	=
   266	G''(r) + {n-1 \over r} G'(r)
   267	\,.
   268	$$
   269	In particular, $\Delta r^k = k (k + n - 2) r^{k-2}$.
   270	If the support of $\psi$ lies in the interior of a ball $B(\bfz, R)$ 
   271	and $\phi(x) = r^k$ with $k > -n + 2$, then letting $D$ be $B(\bfz,
   272	R) \setminus B(\bfz, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon \to 0$ shows that
   273	$\int_{\R^n} \phi \Delta \psi = \int_{\R^n} \psi \Delta \phi$. Similarly,
   274	if $k = - n +2$, then 
   275	$\int_{\R^n} \phi \Delta \psi = \beta_{n-1} \psi(\bfz)$, where
   276	$\beta_{n-1}$ is the surface area of $\sphere^{n-1}$.
   277	
   278	To show that $f_\mu$
   279	determines $\int g \,d\mu$ for all $g \in C^\infty_{\csp}(\R^{2m-1})$, we
   280	now prove that with $c_m := 2(-2\pi)^{m-1} (2m-2)!!$, where $!!$ denotes
   281	the double factorial, we have
   282	$$
   283	\int g \,d\mu = c_m^{-1}
   284	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y)
   285	\,,
   286	$$
   287	where now
   288	$\lambda$ denotes Lebesgue measure on $\R^{2m-1}$. Fubini's theorem
   289	yields
   290	$$
   291	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y) 
   292	=
   293	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) (\Delta^m g)(y)
   294	\, d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
   295	\,.
   296	$$
   297	Applying the preceding Green formulas (translated to $x$)
   298	repeatedly to the inner integral, we obtain
   299	$$\eqaln{
   300	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) (\Delta^m g)(y)
   301	\, d\lambda(y) 
   302	&=
   303	\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \Delta_y^{m-1}
   304	\big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \Delta g(y) \,
   305	d\lambda(y) 
   306	\cr&=
   307	c_m g(x) 
   308	\,,
   309	}$$
   310	as desired.
   311	\Qed
   312	
   313	\eject

   317	transform due to \ref b.Radon/ and \ref b.John:book/, p.~13:

   320	perpendicular to $\omega\in \sphere^{n-1}$, we have
   321	$$

   324	\int_{\sphere^{n-1}} J(\omega,\langle\omega, x\rangle)\,
   325	d\Omega_{n-1}(\omega) &if $n$ is
   326	odd\cr
   327	- (2\pi)^{-n} (-\Delta_x)^{(n-2)/2}
   328	\int_{\sphere^{n-1}} \int_\R {dJ(\omega, p) \over p - \langle\omega,
   329	x\rangle}\, d\Omega_{n-1}(\omega) &if $n$ is
   330	even.\cr}

def lean_verify(
    target: str = "",
    *,
    cwd: str | os.PathLike[str] | None = None,
    mode: str = "project",
) -> LeanVerificationResult:
    project_root, _ = _project_root(cwd)
    root = Path(project_root) if project_root else None
    normalized_mode = str(mode or "project").strip().lower()
    target_path = Path(target).expanduser().resolve() if target else None
    if normalized_mode == "file_exact" and root and target_path:
        try:
            relative = str(target_path.relative_to(root))
        except Exception:
            relative = str(target_path)
        command = ["lake", "env", "lean", relative]
    elif normalized_mode == "module" and root and target_path:
        command = ["lake", "build", _module_name_for_file(root, target_path)]
    else:
        normalized_mode = "project"
        command = ["lake", "build"]
    code, output = _run_command(command, cwd=root)
    result = LeanVerificationResult(
        ok=code == 0,
        mode=normalized_mode,
        command=" ".join(command),
        target=str(target_path or (root or "")),
        output=output,
    )
    append_workflow_outcome("lean-verify", result.to_dict())
    return result

   194	The source proof of the proclaimed theorem is available and should be used by the prover. It is reproduced here from the TeX/PDF extraction, with minor whitespace normalization only.
   195	
   196	```text
   197	Let S be the set of closed half-spaces S ⊂ R^n.
   198	
   199	The Cramer--Wold Theorem. Let μ and ν be Borel probability measures on R^n such that
   200	μ(S) = ν(S) for all S ∈ S. Then μ = ν.
   201	
   202	Proof. Let σ be the (infinite) Borel measure on S that is invariant under isometries,
   203	normalized so that
   204	
   205	  σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) = ‖x‖/2                                      (2.1)
   206	
   207	for ‖x‖ = 1. The measure σ goes back to Crofton (1868) (in two dimensions); it can be
   208	constructed as follows. Let Ω_{n-1} denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
   209	S^{n-1} ⊂ R^n, and let λ denote Lebesgue measure on R. Write
   210	ϕ : S^{n-1} × R → S for the map
   211	
   212	  ϕ(ω,p) := {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}.
   213	
   214	Then σ := α_n · ϕ_*(Ω_{n-1} × λ) for some constant α_n whose value does not concern us.
   215	It is clear that σ is invariant under rotations about the origin and under reflections in
   216	hyperplanes that pass through the origin. Translation invariance amounts to the property
   217	that for y ∈ R^n, the pushforward by ϕ_y(ω,p) := ϕ(ω,p) - y is the same measure. But since
   218	
   219	  ϕ(ω,p) - y
   220	    = {x - y ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}
   221	    = {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x + y> ≥ p}
   222	    = {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p - <ω,y>}
   223	    = ϕ(ω, p - <ω,y>),
   224	
   225	isometry invariance of λ gives this property. The isometry invariance of σ implies that
   226	σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) is a function of ‖x‖ alone; additivity for collinear segments shows that
   227	it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose α_n so that (2.1) holds.
   228	
   229	From (2.1) and isometry invariance, we have
   230	
   231	  ‖x‖ = ∫_S |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 dσ(S).
   232	
   233	Integrating with respect to a signed measure μ on R^n with compact support, we obtain
   234	
   235	  ∫_{R^n} ‖x‖ dμ(x)
   236	    = ∫_S ∫_{R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 dμ(x) dσ(S)
   237	    = ∫_S [1_S(0)(1 - 2 μ(S)) + μ(S)] dσ(S).
   238	
   239	The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another choice and subtracting, we get
   240	
   241	  ∫_{R^n} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) dμ(x)
   242	    = ∫_S [(1_S(y) - 1_S(0))(1 - 2 μ(S))] dσ(S).
   243	
   244	By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed measure μ.
   245	
   246	Define
   247	
   248	  f_μ(y) := ∫_{R^n} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) dμ(x).
   249	
   250	We have shown that the function S ↦ μ(S) determines f_μ. It remains to show that f_μ
   251	determines μ.
   252	
   253	The idea is that if n = 2m - 1 is odd, then Δ^m f_μ = c_m μ for some constant c_m, using
   254	the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, Δ. This then establishes the Cramer--Wold
   255	theorem in odd dimensions. But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension,
   256	the Cramer--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well. That is, we may identify a
   257	measure μ on R^{2m} with a measure μ' on R^{2m} × {0} ⊂ R^{2m+1}. The function S ↦ μ(S)
   258	on half-spaces S ⊂ R^{2m} determines the values μ'(S') for half-spaces S' ⊂ R^{2m+1}.
   259	Since this determines μ', the theorem follows for μ.
